newsitem.title: USA: US, EU planning last ditch try to avert meat trade war.
newsitem.headline: US, EU planning last ditch try to avert meat trade war.

text.p: U.S. and European officials are planning to continue talks next week on meat inspection regulations in a last ditch effort to avert a nasty trade war, a senior U.S. trade official said on Wednesday.

"We're counting on the next talks being (held) next week," U.S. Agriculture Department senior trade adviser Paul Drazek told reporters in a briefing just one day after Washington and Brussels announced separate actions that threatens the trade of hundreds of millions of dollars worth of poultry and meat.

The inability of U.S. and EU officials to reach agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks by an April 1 deadline set into motion moves by both sides that could halt the imports of European meat into the United States and stop U.S. poultry shipments from entering Europe.
An agreement would allow each side to accept meat and poultry from the other even if inspection methods differ.

On Tuesday, Brussels announced it was implementing new standards in all the EU's 15 member nations that would tighten controls on incoming U.S. poultry shipments, and Washington responded by requiring European meat and poultry plants to meet U.S. inspection standards by April 15 or they would not not be able to export to the United States.
The new rules could stop the flow of up to $100 million worth of U.S. poultry and dairy exports and over $300 million worth of EU meat shipments, mainly pork from Denmark.
Drazek said officials are going back to the table to try to come up with a deal before April 15. "The next two weeks we will be trying very hard to get an agreement," he said.

Earlier Wednesday, the senior EU negotiator at the talks sharply criticised Washington's retaliatory action before he headed back to Brussels later in the day, but said that despite the current stand-off, he hoped talks could be restarted soon.
Still, EU official Lars Hoelgaard stressed that the U.S. move to require European plants to meet U.S. requirements was "totally unjustified" and will only make future talks more difficult.
"This will not impress us," said Hoelgaard. "We're not going to just sit back and let the U.S. take these kinds of actions."

Hoelgaard would not comment on what the EU's next move might be, but a European Commission spokesman said earlier in Brussels that the EU has no plans to escalate the trade war, at least for the moment.

Both Hoelgaard and Drazek held out the possibility of taking elements of the bitter trade dispute to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in hopes that the international regulatory body could work something out.
"WTO is clearly an option ... There are some things we are looking at right now as WTO issues," Drazek said.
U.S. industry sources said chances for a settlement to the years-old dispute in the next two weeks are slightly better than two days ago, before each side had played out its hand.

"If you look back in history, we don't get anywhere with the European Union until we take them right to the brink," said Len Condon of the American Meat Institute. Until recently, Condon was for many years an agricultural negotiator at the U.S. Trade Representive's Office and was closely involved in previous negotiations on the issue.
